questions.stem: Before the First World War, the land that became Palestine under the British was ruled by:
options: an independent Arab kingdom based in Damascus under the Hashemite family
the Ottoman Empire, which had held the region since the early 16th century
Egypt, which had governed it as a province since Napoleon's invasion of 1798
Britain, which had controlled it as a protectorate since the opening of the Suez Canal
questions.explanation: The Ottomans conquered the region in 1516-1517 and ruled it for four centuries. Egypt under Muhammad Ali occupied it only briefly in the 1830s, and Britain took it from the Ottomans in 1917-1918.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how the Ottomans governed Palestine in the late 19th century?
options: It was not one province: Jerusalem's district answered to Constantinople and the north to Beirut
It was a single self-governing province with an elected assembly of Muslims, Christians and Jews
It was ruled directly by the Sultan's family from Jerusalem, the empire's second capital city
It was a semi-independent state paying tribute but run by local Christian merchant families
questions.explanation: Ottoman Palestine had no single administration: the district of Jerusalem was governed directly from Constantinople, while the northern districts belonged to the province of Beirut. This is one reason historians say 'Palestine' was a region before it was a political unit.

questions.stem: How did the Ottoman Land Code of 1858 contribute to later tensions in Palestine?
options: It banned all sales of land to non-Muslims, which the British later had to repeal by force
It divided all village land equally among peasant families, ending the power of landlords
It handed all land in the region to the Sultan, so no land could be bought or sold at all
Registration let wealthy, often absentee, landowners gain title to land farmed by peasants
questions.explanation: Many peasants avoided registering land in their own names, so large tracts came to be owned by urban or absentee families. When some of these owners later sold land to Zionist bodies, the tenant farmers who worked it could be evicted, a grievance that fed Arab resentment.

questions.stem: After the Young Turk revolution of 1908, many educated Arabs in the empire turned towards Arab nationalism mainly because:
options: the new rulers abolished Islam as the state religion and closed the religious courts
the new rulers sold the Arab provinces to Britain and France to pay imperial debts
the new rulers moved the capital of the empire from Constantinople to Damascus
the new rulers pushed centralisation and Turkish as the language of government
questions.explanation: The Committee of Union and Progress favoured central control and promoted Turkish, which many Arabs saw as Turkification. Secret societies such as al-Fatat and al-Ahd formed, and an Arab Congress met in Paris in 1913 to demand more autonomy, not yet full independence.

questions.stem: Theodor Herzl is regarded as the founder of political Zionism. In 1896 he published:
options: Auto-Emancipation, a call for Jews to move to Argentina and Russia
The Jewish State, arguing that Jews needed a state of their own
The Basel Program, setting out the rules of the World Zionist Bank
Old New Land, a history of Jewish settlement in Ottoman Palestine
questions.explanation: Herzl's pamphlet Der Judenstaat (The Jewish State) argued that antisemitism would not disappear, so Jews needed a state. Auto-Emancipation was written by Leon Pinsker in 1882, and Old New Land was Herzl's later novel of 1902.

questions.stem: The First Zionist Congress, which created the Zionist Organisation, met in 1897 in:
options: Jerusalem, Palestine
London, England
Vienna, Austria
Basel, Switzerland
questions.explanation: Herzl convened the congress in Basel in August 1897. Its Basel Program called for a home for the Jewish people in Palestine secured by public law.

questions.stem: The First Aliyah (from 1882) brought Jewish settlers to Palestine mainly in response to:
options: an invitation from the Ottoman Sultan to farm unused state land near Jerusalem
the Balfour Declaration and British promises of land for Jewish farmers
the rise of the Nazi Party and new laws against Jews in Germany
pogroms in the Russian Empire after the assassination of Tsar Alexander II
questions.explanation: A wave of pogroms followed the killing of Alexander II in 1881, and groups such as Hovevei Zion (Lovers of Zion) sent settlers to found farming colonies. The Balfour Declaration (1917) and the Nazi era came much later.

questions.stem: The Second Aliyah (1904-1914) is significant mainly because its settlers:
options: were mostly wealthy investors who bought the city of Jerusalem from the Sultan
formed the first Jewish army and fought the Ottomans for control of the whole coast
came mainly from Yemen and Morocco and settled only in the towns of Galilee
founded the first kibbutz and Tel Aviv, and promoted Hebrew labour and language
questions.explanation: Second Aliyah pioneers, largely young socialists from Russia, founded Tel Aviv in 1909 and Degania, the first kibbutz, soon after. They stressed Jewish labour and the revival of Hebrew, and figures such as David Ben-Gurion arrived in this wave.

questions.stem: In the Husayn-McMahon correspondence of 1915-1916, Britain promised Sharif Husayn of Mecca that it would:
options: make him Sultan of the Ottoman Empire after the fall of Constantinople
support Arab independence in return for a revolt against the Ottomans
give him the whole of Egypt and Sudan once the war in Europe was won
let him rule Palestine as a Jewish and Arab state under joint control
questions.explanation: Sir Henry McMahon, British High Commissioner in Egypt, pledged support for Arab independence within limits, and Husayn launched the Arab Revolt in June 1916. Whether Palestine fell within the promised area has been disputed ever since.

questions.stem: Arab leaders argued after 1918 that Britain had broken its promise to them over Palestine. British officials replied that Palestine had been excluded from the Husayn-McMahon pledge. Why could both sides make a case?
options: The letters promised Palestine to both the Arabs and the French in the same paragraph
The letters excluded areas west of Damascus, Homs, Hama and Aleppo without naming Palestine
The letters were written in French, and no Arabic or English copy was ever kept
The letters were signed by Husayn but never by McMahon, so they had no legal force at all
questions.explanation: McMahon excluded 'portions of Syria' lying west of the four towns, which British officials later read as covering Palestine and Arabs read as covering only coastal Lebanon. The ambiguity, not a missing signature, kept the dispute alive.

questions.stem: The Sykes-Picot Agreement of May 1916 was:
options: a secret Anglo-French plan to divide the Ottoman Arab lands into zones
a public treaty granting the Arabs one single state from Syria to Yemen
an Anglo-Zionist plan to make all of Palestine a Jewish state at once
a peace treaty ending the war between Britain and the Ottoman Empire
questions.explanation: Mark Sykes and Francois Georges-Picot agreed on British and French spheres, with much of Palestine under international administration. The Bolsheviks published it in late 1917, and Arabs saw it as a betrayal of the promises made to Husayn.

questions.stem: The Balfour Declaration of 2 November 1917 was a letter from Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour to:
options: Chaim Weizmann
Theodor Herzl
Sharif Husayn
Lord Rothschild
questions.explanation: Balfour wrote to Lord Rothschild, a leader of British Jewry, for passing on to the Zionist Federation. Chaim Weizmann had lobbied for it, and Herzl had died in 1904.

questions.stem: The Balfour Declaration said the British government viewed with favour 'a national home for the Jewish people' in Palestine. What did it say about the Arab majority?
options: Nothing should prejudice the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities
The Arab majority should be moved to Transjordan to make room for Jewish immigration
The Arab majority should decide by referendum whether a Jewish home would be created
The Arab majority would form an independent state alongside the Jewish national home
questions.explanation: The declaration protected the 'civil and religious rights' of 'existing non-Jewish communities' but said nothing of their political or national rights. Arabs noted that the large majority of the population was described only by what it was not.

questions.stem: Historians list several British motives for issuing the Balfour Declaration. Which is LEAST supported by the evidence?
options: A wish to win support from Jews in the USA and Russia for the war effort
A strategic interest in a friendly presence near the Suez Canal after the war
Sympathy for Zionism among leaders such as Lloyd George and Balfour
A plan to hand Palestine to a Jewish state immediately once the war ended
questions.explanation: The declaration promised a vaguely defined 'national home', not a state, and Britain intended to rule Palestine itself. Wartime propaganda aims, imperial strategy near Suez and Christian Zionist sympathy are all well documented motives.

questions.stem: How did most Palestinian Arab leaders respond to the Balfour Declaration and the Mandate that included it?
options: They welcomed both, expecting Jewish investment to bring them independence
They ignored both, since Palestine was then governed from Cairo by the Egyptians
They accepted both in return for British recognition of an Arab state there
They rejected both as a denial of the majority's right to self-determination
questions.explanation: Palestinian congresses and delegations to London demanded its repeal and an elected government. They argued that the Mandate broke Wilson's principle of self-determination and the wartime promises to Husayn.

questions.stem: In January 1919 Emir Faisal signed an agreement with Chaim Weizmann accepting Jewish immigration to Palestine. Why did it have little lasting effect?
options: The Ottoman government refused to recognise it at the Paris Peace Conference
Faisal signed it on condition that no Jewish settlers would live near the coast
Faisal made it conditional on Arab independence, which France then prevented
Weizmann withdrew from it once the Zionists were given Transjordan instead
questions.explanation: Faisal added a note that the agreement depended on the Arabs gaining the independence they had been promised. When France drove him from Damascus in July 1920, the condition failed, and Palestinian Arabs had never endorsed it.

questions.stem: The League of Nations Mandate for Palestine, approved in 1922, differed from other Middle East mandates mainly because it:
options: required Britain to hand Palestine to Transjordan when the mandate ended
included the Balfour Declaration and recognised a Jewish agency to advise Britain
gave Palestine full independence after five years with an elected parliament
placed Palestine under joint British, French and Italian rule from Jerusalem
questions.explanation: The Mandate made Britain responsible for putting the national home policy into effect and recognised a Jewish agency, later the Jewish Agency, to advise the administration. No equivalent Arab body was set up with the same standing.

questions.stem: The riots of August 1929, in which Jews were killed in Hebron and Safed, grew out of a dispute over:
options: the building of a railway between Jerusalem and Jaffa
access to and worship at the Western Wall in Jerusalem
the sale of the port of Haifa to a British oil company
elections to a new legislative council in Jerusalem
questions.explanation: Tensions over Jewish prayer at the Western Wall, beside the Haram al-Sharif, escalated into violence across the country. More than 130 Jews and more than 110 Arabs were killed, many Arabs by British forces.

questions.stem: In 1930 the Passfield White Paper proposed limits on Jewish immigration and land purchase, but in 1931 Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald wrote a letter to Weizmann that in effect reversed it. What does this episode best show?
options: The Zionist movement had abandoned its aims after the violence of the 1929 riots
British policy shifted under pressure from each side, deepening distrust of Britain
Britain had decided to end the Mandate and hand Palestine to the League of Nations
Arab leaders had accepted the national home in return for strict limits on land purchases
questions.explanation: Zionist lobbying in London overturned the Passfield policy within months, and Arabs called the MacDonald letter the 'Black Letter'. The pattern of concession and retreat made both communities doubt British promises.

questions.stem: The Arab Revolt in Palestine began in April 1936 with:
options: an invasion of Palestine by the army of Transjordan
a mutiny by Arab soldiers in the British police force
the assassination of the British High Commissioner
a general strike, soon led by the Arab Higher Committee
questions.explanation: The Arab Higher Committee, led by the Mufti of Jerusalem, Hajj Amin al-Husseini, called a strike that lasted about six months and demanded an end to Jewish immigration. A guerrilla rising followed in 1937-1939.

questions.stem: Which combination best explains the outbreak of the Arab Revolt in 1936?
options: The Peel Commission's partition plan, the 1939 White Paper and the Second World War
The UN Partition Plan, the end of the Mandate and the 1948 Arab-Israeli War
Sharply rising Jewish immigration after 1933, land loss and the death of al-Qassam
The Balfour Declaration's publication, Ottoman taxes and the fall of Jerusalem
questions.explanation: Immigration rose steeply as Jews fled Nazi Germany, raising Arab fears of becoming a minority, while landless peasants were radicalised. The killing of the militant preacher Izz ad-Din al-Qassam by British police in 1935 made him a martyr. The Peel report came after the revolt began.

questions.stem: Historians often argue that the Arab Revolt of 1936-1939 weakened the Palestinian Arabs in 1947-1948. Which point best supports this view?
options: The revolt persuaded Britain to cancel all Jewish immigration permanently after 1939
The revolt united all Palestinian families behind a single elected national leadership
The revolt led Britain to grant the Arabs an independent state in Transjordan in early 1939
British repression killed, jailed or exiled many leaders and left the community disarmed
questions.explanation: Britain crushed the revolt with troops, executions and the exile of leaders, and internal killings divided Palestinian society. The Haganah, by contrast, gained training, partly through cooperation with British forces.

questions.stem: The Peel Commission reported in July 1937 that the Mandate was unworkable and recommended:
options: a federal state with equal numbers of Jewish and Arab ministers under a British governor
handing the whole of Palestine to the League of Nations as an international territory
partition into a small Jewish state, an Arab area joined to Transjordan, and a British zone
an immediate end to Jewish immigration and a single Arab state within twelve months
questions.explanation: Peel proposed the first partition plan: a Jewish state in Galilee and the coastal plain, an Arab state linked to Transjordan, and a British-held corridor from Jerusalem to Jaffa. The Arab leadership rejected it; the Zionist Congress rejected the borders but agreed to negotiate.

questions.stem: Under the 1939 White Paper, Britain announced that:
options: 75,000 Jews could enter over five years, after which immigration would need Arab consent
Palestine would be divided into Jewish and Arab states by the end of the year 1940
Jewish immigration would be unlimited until Jews formed a majority of Palestine's people
the Jewish Agency would govern Palestine alone while Britain fought the war in Europe
questions.explanation: The White Paper of May 1939 also restricted land sales and promised an independent Palestine within ten years. Zionists saw it as a betrayal just as Jews were desperate to escape Nazi Europe; Arab leaders also rejected it.

questions.stem: Why did Britain issue the 1939 White Paper, despite its earlier support for the Jewish national home?
options: The Arab Higher Committee had agreed to accept partition in return for the White Paper
With war near, it wanted to keep Arab and Muslim goodwill in the Middle East and India
It had concluded that the Jewish national home was complete and needed no more migrants
The League of Nations had ordered Britain to end the Mandate within the following year
questions.explanation: Strategic need drove the change: Britain needed the oil, bases and loyalty of Arab states and Muslims across its empire as war with Germany approached. Jewish support in a war against Hitler could be taken for granted.

questions.stem: At the Biltmore Hotel conference in New York in May 1942, Zionist leaders for the first time openly demanded:
options: that Jews be resettled in the USA instead of Palestine
that Britain stay in Palestine permanently as a protector
that Palestine be shared equally with Transjordan's king
that Palestine be established as a Jewish commonwealth
questions.explanation: The Biltmore Program called for unrestricted immigration under Jewish Agency control and a Jewish commonwealth. It marked a shift towards the USA as the movement's main source of support.

questions.stem: How did the Holocaust change the international debate over Palestine after 1945?
options: It persuaded the Arab states to accept unlimited immigration into Palestine
It led Britain to grant Palestine to the Jewish Agency in the summer of 1945
It turned the USA against Zionism, since it wanted survivors to stay in Europe
It won wide sympathy for a Jewish state as a refuge for displaced survivors
questions.explanation: The murder of about six million Jews and the plight of survivors in displaced persons camps strengthened the case for a Jewish state. President Truman urged Britain to admit 100,000 survivors. Arab leaders argued that Palestinians should not pay for crimes committed in Europe.

questions.stem: The bombing of the King David Hotel in Jerusalem in July 1946, which killed 91 people, was carried out by:
options: the Haganah, after a split with the Jewish Agency's leaders
the Irgun, a Jewish underground group fighting British rule
the Arab Higher Committee, in protest at Jewish immigration
the Muslim Brotherhood, sent from Egypt to attack the British
questions.explanation: The hotel housed the British administration's headquarters. The Irgun, led by Menachem Begin, and Lehi waged a campaign of attacks on British targets from 1944, which helped push Britain to give up the Mandate.

questions.stem: Britain referred the Palestine question to the United Nations in 1947 mainly because:
options: Britain had decided to partition Palestine and wanted the UN to pay for it
Jewish insurgency, a costly garrison and US pressure made the Mandate unsustainable
the Arab states had won a short war against Britain and forced it to leave the region
the UN Security Council had ordered Britain to hand all its mandates to the UN
questions.explanation: Exhausted and in debt after the war, Britain faced attacks on its forces, international criticism over the turning back of refugee ships such as the Exodus, and failed talks. Foreign Secretary Bevin handed the problem to the UN.

questions.stem: UNSCOP, the UN committee sent to Palestine in 1947, was made up of representatives of:
options: the Arab League and the Jewish Agency alone
Britain, France and the United States only
eleven member states, including Australia
the five permanent Security Council members
questions.explanation: UNSCOP included Australia, Canada, Czechoslovakia, Guatemala, India, Iran, the Netherlands, Peru, Sweden, Uruguay and Yugoslavia. Great powers were deliberately left out.

questions.stem: UN General Assembly Resolution 181 of 29 November 1947 recommended:
options: a single federal state of Palestine with Jewish and Arab provinces and a shared parliament
a Jewish state in all of Palestine west of the Jordan River, with an Arab state in Transjordan
a ten-year UN trusteeship over the whole of Palestine before any decision on statehood
separate Arab and Jewish states in an economic union, with Jerusalem under international rule
questions.explanation: The majority plan of UNSCOP became Resolution 181, passed by 33 votes to 13 with 10 abstentions. The federal state idea was the UNSCOP minority proposal, and trusteeship was floated by the USA only in early 1948.

questions.stem: Arab leaders rejected the Partition Plan. Which argument was central to their case?
options: The Jewish state was given Jerusalem though most of the city's residents were Arab Christians
The Arab state was denied any coastline, leaving it cut off from trade across the Mediterranean
The Arab state was to be ruled by Britain for twenty years before it could gain independence
The Jewish state was given more than half the land though Jews were about a third of the people
questions.explanation: Arab leaders argued that the plan gave a minority, many of them recent immigrants, more than half the territory, and that the UN could not divide a country against its majority's will. Jerusalem was to be international, and the Arab state had coastline at Gaza and Jaffa.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the Partition Plan was never put into effect?
options: The Security Council vetoed it, so it never became a valid UN resolution
The USA and USSR both voted against it, so no state would accept its terms
Britain would not enforce it, the Arab side rejected it, and fighting broke out at once
The Jewish Agency rejected it, so the UN withdrew the plan in January 1948
questions.explanation: The Jewish Agency accepted the plan, while the Arab Higher Committee and Arab League rejected it. Britain refused to implement a plan one side opposed, the UN had no force to impose it, and civil war began the day after the vote. The USA and USSR both voted in favour.

questions.stem: The State of Israel was proclaimed in Tel Aviv on 14 May 1948 by:
options: Chaim Weizmann
Menachem Begin
Golda Meir
David Ben-Gurion
questions.explanation: Ben-Gurion, head of the Jewish Agency, read the Declaration of Independence as the Mandate ended. Weizmann became the first president, and Begin led the Irgun.

questions.stem: Which development turned the civil war in Palestine into an interstate war in May 1948?
options: The Soviet Union sent troops to defend the new state after the British withdrawal
British forces returned to Palestine to enforce the UN plan against both sides
Turkey invaded from the north to reclaim its former Ottoman provinces of Syria and Palestine
Armies of Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon entered after the Mandate ended
questions.explanation: On 15 May neighbouring Arab states intervened. The war ended with armistice agreements in 1949, which left Israel with more territory than the UN plan, Transjordan holding the West Bank and Egypt holding Gaza.

questions.stem: Which of the following was a reason the Arab states went to war in 1948?
options: A UN Security Council resolution that authorised them to restore the Partition Plan
Promises by Britain to return the Mandate to them if they defeated the Jewish forces
A request from the Jewish Agency to protect Jerusalem's Old City from the advancing Irgun
Public outrage over events such as Deir Yassin, and rivalry over who would gain Palestine
questions.explanation: The killing of villagers at Deir Yassin in April 1948 and the flight of refugees inflamed Arab opinion. The states also competed with one another: King Abdullah of Transjordan wanted to annex Arab Palestine, which Egypt and others opposed.

questions.stem: Palestinians call the events of 1948, in which hundreds of thousands lost their homes, the:
options: Nakba, meaning 'catastrophe'
Intifada, meaning 'uprising'
Hijra, meaning 'migration'
Naksa, meaning 'setback'
questions.explanation: The Nakba is commemorated on 15 May. The Naksa refers to the defeat of 1967, and the Intifadas were uprisings of 1987 and 2000.

questions.stem: Benny Morris, in The Birth of the Palestinian Refugee Problem (1988), challenged the traditional Israeli account of 1948 mainly by arguing that:
options: Britain secretly planned the war in 1948 to keep control of the Suez Canal and Palestine's ports
the exodus came from war and in places expulsions, not chiefly from Arab leaders' orders to leave
no Palestinians left their homes in 1948, and the refugee numbers were invented after the war
the Arab armies were far stronger than the Jewish forces and expected to win within days
questions.explanation: Using newly opened Israeli archives, Morris concluded that the exodus arose from the war itself, with flight from fighting, fear and, in some places, expulsion by Jewish forces. The older Israeli account held that refugees left mainly at the urging of Arab leaders.

questions.stem: Ilan Pappe and Walid Khalidi interpret Plan Dalet, the Haganah's plan of March 1948, differently from Benny Morris. Which statement best describes the difference?
options: They see it as an Arab League plan to invade; Morris sees it as a Jewish plan to accept partition
They see it as a blueprint for expelling Arabs; Morris sees it as a military plan applied unevenly
They see it as a plan to defend Jewish towns only; Morris sees it as a plan to conquer Transjordan
They see it as a British plan to divide Palestine; Morris sees it as a Soviet plan for the region
questions.explanation: Khalidi and Pappe argue that Plan Dalet amounted to a master plan for clearing Arab villages. Morris argues it was a plan to secure territory and roads that gave commanders leeway, with expulsions in some places but no single central order.

questions.stem: A historian argues that the conflict became almost unavoidable once Britain made contradictory promises during the First World War. Which evidence best supports this argument?
options: The Basel Program of 1897 was drawn up with the approval of the Ottoman Sultan
The Mandate gave Palestinians a legislative council that Zionists boycotted
The Peel Commission of 1937 recommended an end to all British rule in the region
Husayn-McMahon, Sykes-Picot and Balfour set incompatible aims for the same land
questions.explanation: The three wartime undertakings pointed to Arab independence, Anglo-French control and a Jewish national home, so each group could claim betrayal. The other options are inaccurate: the Sultan never endorsed Zionism, and Peel proposed a continuing British zone.
